newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-Aer Lingus explores strategic alliance.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Aer Lingus explores strategic alliance.

text.p: Ireland's Aer Lingus said on Wednesday that it was exploring the possibility of entering into a major strategic alliance.

"We have to look at issues such as whether Aer Lingus can continue to trade as a separate, stand-alone entity without a more formal or a more close relationship with some of the partners we might be with right now for tactical or marketing reasons," chief executive Gary McGann told Reuters.

The airline has been mandated by its main shareholder, the Irish government, to consider an alliance against a background of consolidation and globalisation in the industry as a whole and to report back by the end of 1997.
McGann said Aer Lingus was in talks with several parties.
"We are in talks with everybody. Most of the key players that would impact us positively or negatively in our business right now, we are in talks with in one shape or another."
But he said the airline was certainly not at the stage where there's an imminent proposition.

"A critical issue that we have to consider in this regard is whether we can exclude a lot of other business that we currently do with a lot of different players to the benefit of one strong alliance or relationship with one key player or whether we need to find some way of being able to be a little bit more promiscuous," he said.

Earlier, the airline reported a 130 percent rise in 1996 pre-tax profits to 40.9 million Irish pounds, boosted by a sharp drop in the net interest charge and the write-back of year-ago provisions which were no longer required.
Operating profits from continuing businesses rose by a more modest four percent to 41.8 million Irish pounds.

Profits in the core air transport division slipped to 42.2 million Irish pounds from 43.6 million a year earlier as the airline and the industry in general continued to face downward pressure on fares and upward pressure on costs.

"Most of the companies in the industry have to address themselves to that issue of unit costs growing at a greater rate than unit revenue and it's in that context that our margins are down on the air transport side," McGann said.
He said Aer Lingus was currently achieving a return on sales in the airline of around 6.5 percent but would like to be closer to eight or nine percent.
"It's a big challenge for us to get up to that level but certainly what is absolutely unacceptable is that we would have an erosion of where we're at," he said.
Aer Lingus also faces growing competition from private Irish airline Ryanair on its continental European routes.
Ryanair announced in February that it planned to launch new low-fare services from Dublin to Beauvais airport outside Paris and Charleroi outside Brussels on May 1.
"We are certainly aware of it, conscious of it," McGann said. But he added that Aer Lingus had more experience than most in dealing with low-cost, no frills airlines.
He also said Ryanair's entry into Europe was a dramatically different prospect to Ryanair and Aer Lingus competing head to head on a Manchester or Birmingham route.

"It's more analogous to Ryanair-Stansted versus Aer Lingus-Heathrow in that we have a different product, different service, different airport, a capital city airport and we believe a significantly better customer service.
"So we're not going to be offering the same product, same route, same service," he said.
McGann said the airline's main focus this year would be to develop the routes and the options its customers had in terms of where they fly and to enhance service standards.
The airline would also maintain a very strong focus on unit cost reduction and "if we really went for broke, maybe secure a future strategic direction".
